title: Intake Desk
blurb: Every asset and dataset that crosses the desk needs a responsible role before it moves an inch. Route each ticket to the right one.
source: Chapple CISSP SG 10ed ch.5 (Protecting Security of Assets) · April-2024 outline 2.1

roleMatrix.title: Intake Desk
roleMatrix.prompt: Tickets arrive; roles answer. Route each item to the role whose duty it names. Watch the near-misses: owners decide, custodians do, controllers direct, processors obey.

roles.name: Data owner
roles.definition: The person accountable for a body of data — typically a department head or executive who knows its business value. Sets its classification, decides who gets access, and stays answerable for its protection while others do the work.

roles.name: System owner
roles.definition: Owns the platform the data lives on: keeps the system security plan current, ensures controls matching the data's classification are selected and in place, and makes sure operators are trained to run the system securely.

roles.name: Business / mission owner
roles.definition: Owns the business process the systems serve. Weighs security cost against business value, ensures IT actually supports the mission, and answers for the process succeeding — not for any one system or dataset.

roles.name: Data custodian
roles.definition: Delegated the daily care of data by its owner: storing it properly, backing it up and archiving it, applying prescribed labels and controls, and recovering it when something goes wrong. Executes decisions; makes none of them.

roles.name: Data controller
roles.definition: The party that decides WHY personal data is processed and HOW — which data, for what purpose, by what means. Keeps that accountability even when it hires someone else to do the processing.

roles.name: Data processor
roles.definition: Handles personal data strictly on the controller's instructions, commonly as a hired third party. Must protect the data and may not reuse it for its own purposes — the mandate comes entirely from the controller.

roles.name: User
roles.definition: Any person accessing data on a system to get work done. Obliged to touch only what the job requires, follow handling rules for each classification, and comply with policy — access always tracks role and need.

obligations.text: TICKET: A newly acquired customer contact set has no sensitivity level yet, so no handling rule can attach to it. Whose call is the level?
obligations.why: Classifying data is the owner's signature duty — the owner knows the data's importance to the business and sets the level everything else keys off.

obligations.text: TICKET: An analyst wants read access to the sales history archive. The grant needs a yes from whoever answers for that archive.
obligations.why: Permitting access to a dataset is an owner decision; administrators only execute grants the owner has approved.

obligations.text: TICKET: Legal asks who remains accountable for the HR records now that every storage and backup task has been handed to the infrastructure team.
obligations.why: Delegation moves tasks to custodians but never moves accountability — the owner still answers for the data's protection.

obligations.text: TICKET: The payroll platform now hosts data classified two levels higher than before; its documented controls must be re-selected to match.
obligations.why: Ensuring the platform carries controls appropriate to the classification of the data it processes is the system owner's duty, tracked in the system security plan.

obligations.text: TICKET: The security plan for the document server is a year stale and no longer describes the controls actually running. Someone owns that document.
obligations.why: Maintaining an up-to-date system security plan is a defining system-owner responsibility.

obligations.text: TICKET: New operators are joining the records platform and must be trained on its secure operation before they touch it.
obligations.why: The system owner ensures the people operating the system receive appropriate security training — the platform's safe running is their charge.

obligations.text: TICKET: Two departments dispute whether an expensive encryption upgrade for the ordering pipeline is worth the disruption to order fulfilment. Someone owns that trade-off.
obligations.why: Balancing security against business impact for a process is the business/mission owner's call — they answer for the process, so they weigh its trade-offs.

obligations.text: TICKET: A program review asks whether the fleet of systems behind the claims process is actually advancing the business goal it exists for.
obligations.why: Ensuring systems serve the mission is precisely what distinguishes the mission owner from the owners of the individual systems.

obligations.text: TICKET: Funding priorities across the retail process must be set so security spending lands where the business value is. Not a per-system decision.
obligations.why: The mission owner allocates attention and resources at the level of the business process, above any single system or dataset.

obligations.text: TICKET: The overnight backup of the research share failed twice this week; the job must be fixed and a restore proven.
obligations.why: Backing up data and verifying it can be recovered is core custodial work — daily protection tasks delegated by the owner.

obligations.text: TICKET: A crate of drives holding restricted material arrived unmarked; the prescribed sensitivity labels must go on before storage.
obligations.why: Applying the labels the classification scheme prescribes is the custodian's task — the level itself was already decided by the owner.

obligations.text: TICKET: A shared folder was corrupted this morning and yesterday's version must be brought back from the archive.
obligations.why: Recovering lost or corrupted data is squarely custodial: the hands-on care of data through its stored life.

obligations.text: TICKET: The company is launching a loyalty scheme and must decide which member data to collect, for what purpose, and by what means.
obligations.why: Deciding what personal data is processed, why and how is the controller's defining act — purpose and means sit with the controller.

obligations.text: TICKET: Employee payroll data is being handed to an outside bureau to run. One party in this arrangement still directs the processing.
obligations.why: Hiring a processor changes who performs the work, not who directs it — the company collecting its employees' data for payroll remains the controller.

obligations.text: TICKET: The outside payroll bureau receives this month's employee file and must run it exactly as instructed — no more, no less.
obligations.why: A processor acts on behalf of the controller and only on its instructions; the bureau processing another company's employee data fits exactly.

obligations.text: TICKET: A vendor handling client records on instruction proposes mining them for its own marketing. The role's answer must be no.
obligations.why: A processor may not use the controller's data for its own purposes — the mandate is the controller's instructions and nothing beyond.

obligations.text: TICKET: A hosting firm processes personal data purely at another company's direction and must show its safeguards for custody, transport and storage of that data.
obligations.why: Protecting the data while processing on the controller's behalf is the processor's own duty — acting under instruction does not lift the obligation to keep it safe.

obligations.text: TICKET: An employee with legitimate access to the case system has been browsing records unrelated to any assigned case. The role's rules were broken.
obligations.why: Users must access only the data their tasks require; need-to-know binds even people whose credentials technically open the door.

obligations.text: TICKET: A staff member wants to move a sensitive extract onto a personal drive to work from home, against the handling rules for that level.
obligations.why: Complying with handling requirements for classified data in daily work is a user obligation — convenience never overrides the rules the label carries.

obligations.text: TICKET: A new hire needs to be told what the labels on documents mean for how they may copy, store and share them at their desk.
obligations.why: Working with labeled data according to policy is the user's share of asset security — classification labels guide proper use by the people who touch the data.
